artist.artist_description: Patti Page, an American singer born in 1927, was known for her versatile voice that spanned genres like traditional pop, country, and jazz. She rose to fame in the late 1940s with hits like "Tennessee Waltz," which became one of the best-selling singles of the 20th century. Page was the top-charting female vocalist of the 1950s and was nicknamed "The Singin' Rage, Miss Patti Page," and interestingly, she was one of the first artists to use multi-track recording techniques.

Hank Williams was an American singer-songwriter known for his contributions to country music. Born in 1923 in Alabama, he began his career in the late 1930s and quickly rose to fame with hits like "Your Cheatin' Heart" and "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry." Despite his short life, ending at age 29, Williams was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and influenced countless musicians; he was also known for his struggles with alcohol and chronic back pain.

Hank Snow was a Canadian country music artist born in 1914 in Nova Scotia. He began his career performing on local radio and rose to fame with hits like "I'm Moving On," which became a number one hit in 1950. Snow was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1979, and interestingly, he was known for his yodeling style and his custom-designed "Hank Snow White Gospel" guitar.

Pee Wee King, an American musician, was a key figure in the development of country music, particularly known for popularizing the genre through his band, the Golden West Cowboys. Born Julius Frank Anthony Kuczynski in 1914, he started his career in the 1930s and achieved fame with hits like "Tennessee Waltz" and "Slow Poke." Interestingly, King was also instrumental in introducing the accordion to country music and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1974.

Hank Thompson was an American country music singer and songwriter known for his honky-tonk style. Born in Waco, Texas, in 1925, he began his music career after serving in World War II, gaining fame with his 1952 hit "The Wild Side of Life." Thompson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1989 and was known for his energetic live performances and his signature song "Humpty Dumpty Heart."

Kitty Wells, born in Nashville, Tennessee, was an American country music singer known as the "Queen of Country Music." She rose to fame with her 1952 hit "It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels," becoming the first female country singer to have a number one hit. Wells was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1976 and continued performing into her 80s, leaving a lasting legacy in country music.

Jim Reeves was an American country and pop singer born in 1923 in Texas. He began his career in the late 1940s, gaining fame with hits like "He'll Have to Go" and "Welcome to My World." Reeves was posthumously inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1967 after his death in a plane crash in 1964, and he was known for his smooth, velvety voice that helped bridge country and pop music.

Slim Whitman, born in the United States, was a country and western singer known for his yodeling and high-pitched falsetto. He rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "Indian Love Call" and "Rose Marie," and achieved international success, particularly in the UK. Interestingly, Whitman's music was sent to space on the Voyager 1 probe's Golden Record.

Webb Pierce was an American country music artist born in 1921 in West Monroe, Louisiana. He rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "There Stands the Glass" and "In the Jailhouse Now," becoming one of the genre's top stars and known for his flashy Nudie suits. Pierce was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2001, and his song "Slowly" was the first country record to use the echo chamber recording technique.

Tennessee Ernie Ford was an American singer and television host known for his work in country, pop, and gospel music. Born in 1919 in Bristol, Tennessee, he gained fame with his 1955 hit "Sixteen Tons," which became a crossover success. Ford also hosted his own variety show, and a lesser-known fact is that he was a trained classical singer before transitioning to popular music.

George Jones was an American country singer born in Saratoga, Texas, known for his distinctive voice and emotive singing style. He rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "Why Baby Why" and later became known as "No Show Jones" due to his frequent no-shows at concerts during his battle with alcoholism. Jones achieved numerous accolades, including multiple Grammy Awards and induction into the Country Music Hall of Fame.

Elvis Presley, an American singer and actor, was born in Tupelo, Mississippi, and rose to fame in the mid-1950s with his unique blend of rock and roll, country, and gospel music. Known as the "King of Rock and Roll," he achieved numerous milestones, including over 1 billion records sold worldwide and iconic hits like "Hound Dog" and "Jailhouse Rock." Interestingly, Elvis was a twin, but his brother, Jesse Garon Presley, was stillborn.

Marty Robbins was an American singer, songwriter, and racing driver, best known for his contributions to country and western music. Born in 1925 in Arizona, he began his music career after serving in the Navy during World War II, gaining fame with hits like "El Paso," which won the Grammy Award for Best Country & Western Recording in 1961. Robbins was also an avid race car driver, competing in NASCAR, and he holds the distinction of being inducted into both the Country Music Hall of Fame and the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame.

Sonny James, an American country music singer and songwriter, was born in Hackleburg, Alabama, and began his musical career in the early 1950s. Known as the "Southern Gentleman," he achieved significant success with 26 number-one hits on the Billboard country charts, including "Young Love" which also topped the pop charts. A trivia note is that he was the first country artist to receive a gold record for a single, "Young Love," in 1957.

Carl Perkins was an American musician and songwriter known for his pioneering work in rockabilly and rock and roll. Born in Tennessee, he rose to fame with his 1956 hit "Blue Suede Shoes," which became one of the first records to sell over a million copies. Interestingly, Perkins wrote the song after hearing a soldier say, "Don't step on my blue suede shoes," which inspired the iconic lyrics.

Ray Price was an American country music singer, songwriter, and guitarist known for his significant contributions to the genre. Born in Texas in 1926, he began his career in the late 1940s and became famous for his honky-tonk style and later his smooth, orchestral "countrypolitan" sound. Price's key achievements include his hit songs like "Crazy Arms" and "For the Good Times," and he was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1996; trivia includes that he served in the U.S. Marines during World War II.

Johnny Cash was an American singer-songwriter known for his deep, distinctive voice and his genre-blending style that encompassed country, rockabilly, and gospel. Born in Arkansas in 1932, he rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "I Walk the Line" and "Folsom Prison Blues," the latter recorded live at a prison concert. Cash's iconic "Man in Black" persona and his advocacy for the downtrodden, including his performances in prisons, cemented his legacy as a cultural icon.

The Everly Brothers, Don and Phil, were American musicians known for their close harmony singing in the rock and roll and country genres. They rose to fame in the late 1950s with hits like "Bye Bye Love" and "Wake Up Little Susie," significantly influencing the Beatles and other artists. A notable trivia is that they were among the first 10 inductees into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1986.

Jerry Lee Lewis, an American musician, was a pioneer in rock and roll, known for his energetic performances and hits like "Great Balls of Fire." Born in Louisiana in 1935, he began playing piano at a young age and rose to fame in the 1950s. Despite personal controversies, he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and continued performing into his 80s, famously known for marrying his 13-year-old cousin, which caused a significant scandal.

Don Gibson was an American country music singer and songwriter born in 1928 in North Carolina. He rose to fame in the 1950s with hits like "Oh Lonesome Me" and "I Can't Stop Loving You," the latter becoming a major success for Ray Charles. Gibson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2001, and his songs have been covered by numerous artists across various genres.

Johnny Horton was an American singer-songwriter known for his work in country and rockabilly music. Born in Los Angeles in 1925, he gained fame in the 1950s with hits like "The Battle of New Orleans," which won a Grammy Award. Interestingly, Horton was also a keen amateur pilot and tragically died in a car accident in 1960 at the age of 35.

Tex Williams, an American country and western swing musician, was born in 1917 in Illinois. He gained fame as the lead singer of Spade Cooley's band before launching a successful solo career with hits like "Smoke! Smoke! Smoke! (That Cigarette)." Williams was known for his distinctive voice and humorous stage presence, and he was inducted into the Western Music Association Hall of Fame in 1999.

Red Foley, born in Kentucky, USA, was a prominent country music singer and songwriter known for his contributions to the genre in the mid-20th century. He began his career in the 1930s, gaining fame through radio shows and later becoming one of the first country artists to cross over to pop charts with hits like "Chattanoogie Shoe Shine Boy." Foley was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1967, and interestingly, he also hosted the first-ever CMA Awards show in 1967.

Ernest Tubb was an American country music singer and songwriter known for popularizing the honky-tonk style. Born in Texas in 1914, he overcame early career struggles to become a Grand Ole Opry member and a major influence on country music. Tubb's signature song, "Walking the Floor Over You," became a hit in 1941, and he was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1965.

Leon Payne was an American country music singer and songwriter born in 1917 in Alba, Texas. He began his career in the 1930s, gaining fame with songs like "Lost Highway" and "I Love You Because," the latter becoming a hit for Elvis Presley. Payne overcame blindness caused by a childhood accident to become a significant figure in country music, and he was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970.
